fa: Earth's highest peak above sea level; its summit is made of marine limestone, a reminder that it once lay at the bottom of an ancient sea.
The second-highest mountain on Earth and widely considered the deadliest of the 8000ers, nicknamed the 'Savage Mountain' for its brutal weather.
The first British climbers to reach the top stopped a few meters short of the true summit, honoring a promise to the local Sikkimese who consider it sacred.
Connected to Everest by the South Col, its name means 'South Peak' in Tibetan; the two mountains share much of the same climbing route.
Its distinctive four-sided pyramid shape makes it one of the most technically demanding 8000ers to climb.
Considered the easiest of the 8000ers to climb, its name means 'Turquoise Goddess' in Tibetan.
fc: 1954, Herbert Tichy, Joseph Joechler and Pasang Dawa Lama

fa: Held the title of world's highest known mountain from 1808 to 1838 before Kangchenjunga and then Everest were measured.
Its name comes from the Sanskrit for 'mountain of the spirit'; it is sometimes called the 'Japanese mountain' for the many Japanese expeditions that pioneered its routes.
Nicknamed 'Killer Mountain' after claiming dozens of lives during early 20th-century expeditions before its first successful ascent, made solo.
The first 8000-meter peak ever climbed, but statistically still one of the most dangerous due to a very high fatality-to-summit ratio.
Also known as Hidden Peak because it is tucked away from view behind other Karakoram giants.
Named for its wide, roughly 1.5 km long summit ridge, clearly visible from base camp near K2.
fc: 1957, Fritz Wintersteller, Marcus Schmuck, Kurt Diemberger and Hermann Buhl

fa: Generally regarded as one of the more approachable 8000ers, making it a common choice for climbers attempting their first peak above 8000 meters.
fc: 1956, Fritz Moravec, Josef Larch and Hans Willenpart

fa: The only 8000-meter peak located entirely within a single country, Tibet; it was the last of the 8000ers to be climbed due to Chinese access restrictions.
Often called the 'Matterhorn of the Himalayas' for its dramatic pointed shape and hanging glacier, considered one of the most beautiful mountains on Earth.
fc: 1961, Mike Gill, Barry Bishop, Wally Romanes and Mike Ward

fa: Long the highest peak within the borders of British India; a surrounding sanctuary of peaks was considered so sacred and remote that it was closed to climbers for decades.

Nicknamed 'Fishtail' for its twin-pronged summit; considered sacred to the god Shiva, climbing to its true top has been forbidden by the Nepalese government since a 1957 expedition stopped short of the summit by agreement.
Considered sacred by four religions, including Hinduism and Buddhism; out of respect for that belief, no confirmed ascent to its summit has ever been made.
Nicknamed the 'Father of Ice Mountains'; its gentle, rounded slopes make it one of the highest peaks on Earth that can be climbed on skis.
The highest peak in the Hindu Kush range and outside the Himalaya-Karakoram system; local legend held its summit was home to fairies who punished trespassers.
The highest point in the former Soviet Union, it was renamed several times through history, once honoring Lenin and later Communism itself before its current name.
Its marble summit pyramid catches the low sun in a deep blood-red glow, a striking effect that inspired its nickname 'Blood Mountain'.
The northernmost peak above 7000 meters on Earth, and one of the coldest and most avalanche-prone high mountains in the world.
The highest peak in Sichuan province, so remote that it was misjudged for years to rival Everest in height before accurate surveys corrected the record.
Western Europe's highest peak; its first ascent is credited with sparking the modern sport of mountaineering.
One of the most photographed mountains in the world; its dramatic first ascent ended in tragedy when four climbers fell to their deaths during the descent.
Its notorious North Face, nicknamed 'Mordwand' (murder wall), was not climbed until 1938 after claiming several climbers' lives in earlier attempts.
Home to Europe's highest railway station, built inside the mountain and reachable by a rack railway completed in 1912.
fc: 1811, Johann Rudolf Meyer and Hieronymus Meyer

fa: The highest peak located entirely within Switzerland, since taller neighbors like the Matterhorn and Monte Rosa sit on the Italian border.
fc: 1858, John Llewelyn Davies with local guides

fa: Once described by a pioneering alpinist as the most beautiful mountain in the Alps for its near-perfect pyramidal shape.
The highest peak of the Eastern Alps and the only peak above 4000 meters outside the Western Alps.
Austria's highest peak; a scenic high-alpine road built in the 1930s now winds close to its base and is one of Europe's most famous mountain drives.
fc: 1800, expedition organized by Bishop Franz Xaver von Salm-Reifferscheidt

fa: Germany's highest peak; three countries, Germany, Austria and Switzerland, are all visible from its summit on a clear day.
Its 1854 ascent by an English lawyer is traditionally cited as the spark that ignited the 'Golden Age of Alpinism', a wave of British enthusiasm for Alpine climbing.
The highest peak of the Pyrenees, its small summit glacier is one of the last remnants of ice still clinging to the range.
fc: 1842, Platon de Tchihatchef and Jean-Pierre Sanio

fa: Slovenia's highest peak and a national symbol, featured on the country's flag and coat of arms.
fc: 1778, four Carniolan explorers commissioned by Baron Sigmund Zois

fa: Nicknamed the 'Giant of Provence', it is famous today as one of the most feared climbs of the Tour de France cycling race.
fc: 1336, Petrarch, described in one of the earliest known accounts of mountaineering for its own sake

fa: The highest peak in Scandinavia; a small summer ski resort operates near its base even at the height of summer, using a permanent snowfield.
The highest peak of the Carpathian mountain range and of Slovakia, standing well above the rest of the surrounding High Tatras.
In Georgian legend this dormant volcanic peak is where Amirani, a Prometheus-like hero, was chained by the gods for stealing fire.
The highest peak in the Balkan Peninsula, its name is believed to derive from a Persian phrase meaning 'near God'.
The highest peak of the Apennines, home to the southernmost glacier in continental Europe, now one of the smallest ice bodies on the continent.
Greece's highest peak, believed in ancient mythology to be the home of the twelve Olympian gods.
fc: 1913, Christos Kakkalos with Frederick Boissonnas and Daniel Baud-Bovy

fa: The highest peak of the Indian Ocean islands, its name means 'Peak of the Snows' even though snow there is exceptionally rare.
A dormant volcanic peak believed to be depicted in a roughly 8000-year-old wall painting at the Neolithic settlement of Catalhoyuk, possibly the oldest known landscape artwork.
North America's highest peak; it has one of the greatest base-to-summit rises of any mountain on Earth, towering nearly 5500 meters above its surrounding plain.
Canada's highest peak has such an enormous summit plateau that its true highest point was only confirmed by GPS survey in the early 1990s.
The highest peak in the Canadian Rockies, often shrouded in its own weather system and cloud cap even on clear days.
fc: 1913, William Foster, Curly Phillips and Conrad Kain

fa: The highest peak entirely within British Columbia, it went unclimbed for years after being nicknamed 'Mystery Mountain' by early surveyors.
fc: 1936, Fritz Wiessner and William P. House

fa: Nicknamed the 'Matterhorn of the Rockies' for its strikingly similar pyramidal shape to its famous Swiss counterpart.
Rises dramatically straight from the valley floor with no foothills, giving it one of the most striking silhouettes of any peak in the United States.
fc: 1898, William Owen, Franklin Spalding, Frank Petersen and John Shive

fa: The highest point in Rocky Mountain National Park, its sheer east face called 'The Diamond' is one of the most celebrated big-wall climbs in the US.
The highest peak in the contiguous United States; remarkably, it lies only about 136 km from Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America.
fc: 1873, Charles Begole, A.H. Johnson and John Lucas

fa: This granite landmark in Yosemite Valley was long declared unclimbable until a blacksmith rigged an eyebolt ladder up its final smooth slope.
The view from its summit inspired the lyrics to 'America the Beautiful'; a cog railway has carried visitors to the top since 1891.
Measured from its base on the ocean floor, it is the tallest mountain on Earth at over 10000 meters, taller than Everest, though most of it lies underwater.
Marks the northern terminus of the Appalachian Trail; its Native Penobscot name means 'Greatest Mountain'.
fc: 1804, Charles Turner Jr., the first recorded non-native ascent

fa: The highest peak east of the Mississippi River is named after a scientist who died in a fall while trying to prove it was the tallest in the region.
New York State's highest peak; a small pond just below its summit is considered the highest source of the Hudson River.
fc: 1837, surveying expedition led by Ebenezer Emmons

fa: The highest peak outside Asia, making it one of the celebrated Seven Summits, one for each continent.
Because Earth bulges at the equator, its summit is the point on our planet's surface farthest from the planet's center, farther than even Everest.
fc: 1880, Edward Whymper, Jean-Antoine Carrel and Louis Carrel

fa: Peru's highest peak; a catastrophic avalanche from its slopes in 1970 buried the town of Yungay below, one of the deadliest mountain disasters in history.
Its jagged granite spire is so distinctive that its silhouette became the logo of an outdoor clothing brand.
For decades a disputed 1959 summit claim was debated by climbers, until a widely accepted first true ascent was finally made 15 years later.
Bolivia's highest peak, an extinct volcanic cone surrounded by the world's highest forest, made up of hardy Polylepis trees growing above 4000 meters.
fc: 1939, Joseph Prem, H. Awerzger and F. Kutschera

fa: Venezuela's highest peak carries a bronze bust of Simon Bolivar at its summit, hauled up piece by piece and installed in 1951.
This flat-topped tepui with sheer cliffs on all sides inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's novel 'The Lost World' about a plateau where prehistoric creatures survived.
Costa Rica's highest peak; on an exceptionally clear day, both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea can reportedly be seen from its summit.
Africa's highest peak and the world's tallest free-standing mountain, rising alone from surrounding plains rather than as part of a mountain range.
Despite sitting almost exactly on the equator, its higher peaks still carry glaciers, though they have shrunk dramatically in the past century.
Its glacier-capped summit, Margherita Peak, sits almost on the equator in one of Africa's rainiest and most persistently cloud-covered ranges.
Its famously flat summit plateau is often capped by a cloud formation locals call the 'tablecloth' when moist air spills over its edge.
fc: 1503, Antonio de Saldanha, the earliest recorded ascent

fa: Ethiopia's highest peak sits within a range so rugged early European explorers nicknamed it the 'Africa's Grand Canyon', home to rare wildlife like the gelada monkey.
The highest island peak in the world and, remarkably, still carries small equatorial glaciers, though they are rapidly disappearing.
New Zealand's highest peak, sacred to the Maori as an ancestor figure; a rockfall and ice avalanche shortened its summit by several meters in 1991.
fc: 1894, Tom Fyfe, James Clarke and George Graham

fa: This near-perfectly symmetrical volcanic cone so closely resembles Mount Fuji that filmmakers have used it as a stand-in for the Japanese peak.
Mainland Australia's highest peak is also one of the easiest to reach among the world's continental high points, with a walking track leading close to its summit.
The highest peak in Papua New Guinea, occasionally dusted with frost despite lying just a few degrees south of the equator.
Antarctica's highest peak was not even discovered until aerial surveys in 1958, and remained unclimbed for another eight years after that.
Europe's highest peak is a dormant volcano with twin summits; it is counted among the Seven Summits under the common definition of Europe's borders.
fc: 1829, Killar Khashirov, first recorded ascent of the east summit

fa: The highest peak in the British Isles; a former observatory once staffed year-round near its summit recorded some of Britain's most extreme weather.
The highest peak between the Himalayas and New Guinea, home to thousands of plant species found nowhere else on Earth.
Mexico's highest peak and North America's third-highest; its glacier-capped, near-symmetrical cone was once used as a navigational landmark by sailors far out in the Gulf of Mexico.
Revered in Jewish, Christian and Islamic tradition as the mountain where Moses received the Ten Commandments; a monastery has stood at its base since the 6th century.
